ov: Austen’s novel of manners follows Elizabeth Bennet’s education in self-knowledge as pride and prejudice give way to understanding. In a Critical Study, you argue about its literary value: ironic narration, free indirect discourse, a tightly controlled marriage plot and a moral vision that holds together money, reason and love.
rub: Reader, author, text and context: how Regency attitudes to marriage, money and class shape the plot.
Aesthetic qualities, structure and language: irony, aphorism, free indirect discourse and symmetry.
Conventions: the novel conforms to the marriage plot, yet challenges its assumptions about love, rank and women’s choices.
sum: Elizabeth Bennet, one of five daughters of a gentleman whose estate is entailed away from them, meets the wealthy Mr Darcy when Bingley rents Netherfield. Darcy’s pride and Elizabeth’s prejudice, fed by the charming Wickham’s lies, lead her to refuse Darcy’s first proposal. His letter reveals the truth, and Elizabeth reassesses herself. After Lydia’s elopement with Wickham threatens the family’s reputation, Darcy quietly secures the marriage. Jane and Bingley reunite, Lady Catherine’s attempt to stop the match fails, and Darcy and Elizabeth marry, each humbled and wiser.
acts: Netherfield is let. Darcy slights Elizabeth at the ball, Wickham tells his lies, Collins proposes and is refused, Charlotte accepts him, and Bingley leaves.
At Hunsford, Darcy proposes and is rejected. His letter exposes Wickham and Darcy’s part in separating Jane and Bingley.
At Pemberley Elizabeth’s view of Darcy shifts. Lydia elopes, Darcy intervenes, Bingley returns, Lady Catherine confronts Elizabeth and the second proposal is accepted.
ch: Elizabeth Bennet
Heroine
Quick-witted and proud of her judgement; her arc is learning her own blindness.
Till this moment I never knew myself.
Mr Darcy
Wealthy landowner
Proud and reserved, then humbled. He shows growth through action as well as speech.
She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me.
Mr Bennet
Elizabeth’s father
Ironic and detached; fails his duty as a parent.
For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?
Mrs Bennet
Elizabeth’s mother
Anxious and comic; her obsession reflects real economic danger.
(Narrator) The business of her life was to get her daughters married.
Charlotte Lucas
Elizabeth’s friend
Pragmatic; she accepts Collins for security.
Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.
cx: Jane Austen (1775–1817), a clergyman’s daughter who never married, drafted this novel as First Impressions in the 1790s and published it in 1813. Her family’s dependence on relatives gave her first-hand knowledge of marriage and money.

Novel of manners and the rise of the novel; Enlightenment reason and sensibility debates; conduct books shaped ideas of female behaviour. Irony and free indirect discourse are Austen’s signature techniques.
Regency England during the Napoleonic Wars; the militia quartered in Meryton enables Wickham’s elopement plot. Landed gentry hold power while trade money rises.
Class rank decides worth; the entail keeps Longbourn from the Bennet women, so marriage is financial survival. Women’s reputations are fragile: Lydia’s scandal threatens all her sisters.
im: Imagery patterns: eyes, looks and windows (reading others); letters (truth arrives on paper); gardens and walking (freedom and judgement).
The portrait gallery at Pemberley: Elizabeth sees Darcy’s portrait and her feelings shift, so a visual image changes her understanding.
Hugh Thomson’s 1894 illustrations and later screen adaptations (the 1995 BBC lake scene) shaped popular images of Darcy and Elizabeth that students can compare with Austen’s restrained prose.

q.m: Question link: integrity and literary value.

A.i: Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice investigates stability and disruption through the imaginative architecture of the marriage plot: the entail, Darcy’s first proposal and Lydia’s elopement threaten the Bennets’ security, yet Elizabeth’s growth and the novel’s ordered resolution restore a more honest stability. Writing in Regency England, where women’s futures depended on marriage and property, Austen uses irony and free indirect discourse to expose the fragility of social order. Through economic insecurity, emotional upheaval and self-knowledge, the novel suggests that true stability must be earned.
b: Austen establishes stability as precarious and economic. The opening aphorism, “a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife”, mocks society’s assumptions with ironic mock-grandeur, while the narrator’s deadpan remark that “the business of her life was to get her daughters married” reduces Mrs Bennet’s anxiety to a commercial pursuit that hints at the entail’s real threat. Charlotte’s claim that “happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance” shows how limited women’s security was. Stability is a social fiction the plot will test.

Disruption arrives through emotion and scandal. Darcy’s proposal, “My feelings will not be repressed”, uses short declaratives and the passive voice to show pride cracking, yet his insulting manner shatters Elizabeth’s composure. Lydia’s elopement then threatens every Bennet sister’s reputation, and Mr Bennet’s complacent “For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours” exposes the cost of his indifference. These disturbances show that social order rests on reputation, which the plot imperils.

Stability returns through self-knowledge, not simply marriage. Elizabeth’s epiphany, “Till this moment I never knew myself”, uses monosyllabic diction to mark the novel’s pivot, while Darcy’s confession, “I have been a selfish being all my life”, shows his growth in his own voice. The Pemberley portrait gallery, where an image changes Elizabeth’s view of Darcy, links vision with understanding. The final marriages therefore restore order on a more honest basis, completing the argument.
A.c: Austen therefore shows that stability in her world is fragile, disturbed by economic law, emotional pride and scandal, and restored only through self-knowledge. The novel’s ironic voice and balanced structure give disruption a moral purpose, leaving readers to value an order that is earned rather than inherited.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis answers “how” (through the imaginative aspects), each paragraph uses three examples, techniques are named with effects, and context (entail, Regency marriage) is built into the analysis rather than added on.

B.i: In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen explores stability and disruption through the marriage plot. The Bennet family’s security is threatened, but it is restored at the end.
b: At the start, Austen shows that stability depends on money. The opening line, “a truth universally acknowledged”, is ironic because it mocks society’s attitude to marriage. Charlotte says that “happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance”, which shows that women had few choices.

Disruption happens when Darcy proposes and when Lydia elopes. Darcy says, “My feelings will not be repressed”, which shows his pride. Mr Bennet says, “For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours”, which shows he is not a good father.
Stability returns when Elizabeth says, “Till this moment I never knew myself.” This shows she has changed. Darcy also says he has been “a selfish being all my life”, which shows he has changed too.
B.c: In conclusion, Austen shows that stability is threatened but restored. Elizabeth and Darcy marry and the novel ends happily.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes and a clear structure, but techniques are only occasionally named and the analysis is general. The question’s “imaginative aspects” and “investigated” are not addressed directly.

models.C: In Pride and Prejudice the Bennets need money. Darcy proposes to Elizabeth and she says no. Lydia runs away. In the end, Elizabeth marries Darcy. Austen uses irony to show stability and disruption.
models.D: Pride and Prejudice is about Elizabeth and Darcy who fall in love. There are problems but they get married.

A.i: Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice has earned its literary value through the union of artistry and integrity: an ironic, finely balanced craft that is matched by a moral vision that refuses easy romance. Through the narrator’s epigrams, her symmetrical structure and her credible characters, Austen both entertains and tests the values of Regency society. My understanding of the novel’s value is that it lasts because its form and its ethics are inseparable.
b: Austen’s artistry begins with her ironic narrative voice. The opening aphorism, “a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife”, announces the marriage plot while mocking society’s assumptions, and “the business of her life was to get her daughters married” reduces Mrs Bennet to a commercial obsession in a single deadpan phrase. This economy of irony makes the novel funny, but it also lets Austen expose social pressure without sermon. The craft therefore deepens my appreciation of the text’s value as social comedy and critique.

Austen’s integrity lies in refusing to let love ignore money and reason. Charlotte’s “happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance” counters Elizabeth’s idealism with realism, and Mr Bennet’s “For what do we live, but to make sport for our neighbours” shows the moral cost of irony without responsibility. Elizabeth’s “Till this moment I never knew myself” and Darcy’s admission of being “a selfish being all my life” show both characters earning their happiness through self-examination. The novel’s moral coherence, where growth is earned and consequences are real, convinces me of its integrity.

Structure and reception reinforce this value. The three-volume symmetry of two proposals, the second answering the first, and the Pemberley portrait gallery, where an image shifts Elizabeth’s view of Darcy, let Austen link form to theme. Admittedly her world is narrow, confined to the gentry, which may limit its scope. Yet the novel’s enduring adaptation, from illustration to screen, suggests that its human questions, about pride, judgement and the price of security, remain universal.
A.c: In evaluating Austen’s artistry and integrity, I conclude that Pride and Prejudice’s literary value lies in the inseparability of its craft and its conscience. Its irony entertains, its structure persuades, and its moral honesty ensures that its judgement of human nature still feels true.
A.n: What to notice: the response evaluates (gives a verdict, even acknowledging a limitation), keeps “artistry” and “integrity” in view, includes context and reception, and ties the analysis to “my understanding” of value.

B.i: In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen uses artistry and integrity to give the novel literary value. Through irony and realistic characters, Austen creates a lasting story.
b: Austen’s artistry is shown through irony. The opening line, “a truth universally acknowledged”, is funny because it mocks how society thinks about marriage. The narrator says, “The business of her life was to get her daughters married”, which makes Mrs Bennet seem silly. This shows Austen’s skill in humour.

Austen’s integrity is shown through her characters. Charlotte says, “Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance”, which shows the reality of marriage. Elizabeth says, “Till this moment I never knew myself”, and Darcy says he has been “a selfish being all my life”, which shows that they change.
The novel has value because it has a clear structure and a happy ending. The Pemberley portrait shows how Elizabeth’s view of Darcy changes. This shows that the novel is well planned.
B.c: In conclusion, Austen’s artistry and integrity give the novel literary value. It is still enjoyed today.
B.n: What to notice: relevant evidence, but it describes rather than evaluates. There is no weighing of limitations, “influenced your understanding” is not addressed, and the conclusion is general.

What is the entail and why does it matter?
A legal rule leaving Longbourn to a male heir (Mr Collins), so the Bennet daughters need marriages.
Till this moment I never knew myself (Ch 36).
